notes: Operator asked for ARIA to run in ultracode mode. `max` is the deepest CLI reasoning level, verified against Claude Code 2.1.220 (--effort low|medium|high|xhigh|max), and was DEAD in this repo: DEFAULT_EFFORT was xhigh, the credit fallback hardcoded xhigh, and zero of the 20 aria-*.md declared it. All 20 now declare effort: max, with DEFAULT_EFFORT and CREDIT_FALLBACK_EFFORT raised to match so the fail-safe resolves UPWARD and an unparseable frontmatter field can never quietly run shallower than policy. Non-ARIA platform reviewers were deliberately LEFT at xhigh: the request scoped to ARIA, and raising 84 unrelated agents is a separate decision with its own latency profile -- an over-broad edit to the shared jest branch caught exactly that and was reverted. THE SECOND HALF IS THE MORE IMPORTANT ONE. The operator's instruction was to plan with fable and implement with opus, which is inverted relative to this repo: fable IS the expensive, most-capable tier (priced 2x opus in MODEL_PRICING_USD_PER_MTOK; DEFAULT_MODEL fails safe to it precisely because it is the most expensive; MODEL_FALLBACK_TIER = {fable: opus} means opus is what you fall back TO), and the K5 tier flip of 2026-07-01 deliberately moved writers ONTO fable. Implementers are therefore ALREADY on the best model. The likely cause of the inversion is documented drift, which this change fixes: agent-frontmatter-schema.spec.ts:133-146 still said writers 'stay on opus/xhigh' while its own assertion three lines later said toBe('fable'); .claude/README.md, _maintenance/prompt-writer.md and plans 023 + 030 said the same. Anyone reading the prose would conclude opus was the write tier. The model swap was NOT performed: it would downgrade the write path to the cheaper tier, strip its credit-fallback pool (opus has no MODEL_FALLBACK_TIER entry, so an exhaustion now raises terminally), silently drop the 2x budget reservation multiplier keyed on the literal alias 'fable', and require overriding two mirrored invariants whose stated purpose is to prevent exactly that.

title: The model fallback was a single hardcoded hop: audit rows named fable->opus@xhigh as a literal and the budget multiplier keyed on the alias string
rule_violated: Anything derived from a topology must be computed from it. A hardcoded copy of one hop becomes a false statement the moment the topology changes, and a false statement in an append-only ledger cannot be corrected.
notes: Operator defined a two-rung ladder: planning runs fable falling back to opus, implementation runs opus falling back to the latest sonnet. Implementing it exposed three places that had encoded the single fable->opus hop as data-in-prose. (1) GOVERNANCE AUDIT ROWS: ci_executor.py emitted "to_model": "opus", "to_effort": "xhigh" and the stage string 'fable->opus@xhigh'; worker_executor.py wrote the same to stderr. With the write tier on opus these would have recorded a fable->opus hop that never happened, into an append-only hash-chained ledger -- the one artifact in this system that cannot be corrected afterwards. Both now derive from MODEL_FALLBACK_TIER and CREDIT_FALLBACK_EFFORT. (2) BUDGET RESERVATION: ci_executor.py:741 multiplied the reservation by 2x when resolve_claude_model(agent) == 'fable', because fable prices at 2x opus. The literal comparison silently returned a 1x reservation the moment the write tier moved off fable, and would need editing again at the next tier change. It now derives the ratio from MODEL_FAMILY_PRICING_USD_PER_MTOK against the opus-calibrated baseline, comparing output rates since agent envelopes are output-dominated, and still falls back to a conservative 2x on any lookup failure. (3) TESTS ENCODING THE OLD SHAPE: two tests used opus as their example of a tier with no fallback, which stopped being true; they now use sonnet, the ladder terminus, and a new test covers the opus->sonnet rung directly. The ladder is also asserted acyclic, which was not a possible failure while it had one hop. NOTE ON THE TIER DECISION: moving writers from fable to opus is a move to the cheaper tier by this repo's own pricing (fable is 2x opus) and reverses the K5 flip of 2026-07-01. It is safe specifically BECAUSE the operator added the opus->sonnet rung -- before it, opus was a leaf and ORPHAN-HIGH-475 made an exhausted implementer raise terminally. The two mirrored write-tier invariants were retargeted to opus rather than deleted, so a frontmatter edit still cannot silently drop a writer below its assigned tier.

title: A NameError on the only real worker-dispatch path shipped with 2905 passing tests, and the first two detectors written for it were themselves theatre
rule_violated: A remediation branch must not reproduce the defect class it exists to close. Unreachable-at-runtime code cannot be validated by a green suite, and a detector must be proven against the defect it targets before it is trusted.
notes: Found by a 14-agent adversarial audit of this branch's own S1-S9 work, confirmed by two independent verifiers. The final commit of the tier-ladder work (c824de214) introduced `MODEL_FALLBACK_TIER.get(model, ...)` into worker_executor.main(), where `model` is bound ONLY as a parameter of the nested _dispatch_attempt(model, effort) defined above it. That is an unconditional NameError on the only real worker dispatch path, and `aria:test:unit` reported 2905 OK both before AND after the fix, because no test exercises that callsite -- verbatim the defect class this whole branch exists to close, reproduced by the remediation itself. Fixed to profile.model, the binding the run_with_model_fallback call 17 lines below already uses. THE DETECTOR HISTORY IS THE MORE USEFUL RECORD. A static unbound-name resolver was added so the class becomes detectable rather than the instance merely fixed, and the FIRST TWO versions of it passed with the NameError deliberately reintroduced: (1) _scope_bindings used ast.walk, which pulled a NESTED function's parameters into the enclosing scope's binding set, so `model` looked bound in main(); (2) the replacement recursion inspected each node's CHILDREN but never the node itself, so a function-local `from x import y` bound nothing and the checker produced three false positives on real code instead. Only the third version both passes clean and fails on the reintroduced bug (worker_executor.py:259 `model` loaded in main() but bound nowhere reachable). The lesson generalises beyond this file: a detector that has not been run against the defect it targets is indistinguishable from one that works, which is why every fix on this branch is now verified by reverting the production callsite rather than by a green suite. Scope: the resolver covers worker_executor.py, ci_executor.py and claude_runtime.py -- the three modules on ARIA's live spawn path.

title: The run_with_model_fallback docstring described the pre-ladder single-hop policy on five counts after the code had moved on
rule_violated: Prose that describes a control must agree with the control. A docstring contradicting its own function is read as authoritative and is the same defect as a stale test comment.
notes: Found by the adversarial audit. After the ladder and the fail-closed raise landed, the docstring still said: fallback fires ONLY when the primary model is fable; the retry is on opus at xhigh; each branch returns the opus result directly; a credit/refusal signal on that result escalates at the caller; and a failure on a non-fable model is returned unchanged. All five were false -- the ladder is a map, the effort is CREDIT_FALLBACK_EFFORT, and an unrecoverable exhaustion RAISES ClaudeCreditExhausted rather than returning. The fourth claim was the dangerous one because it asserted an escalation path that does not exist: no caller reads credit_exhaustion off the returned value, which is exactly the ORPHAN-HIGH-475 defect the raise was added to close. Two commits earlier I criticised precisely this pattern in the jest tier comments (ORPHAN-MEDIUM-477) and then reproduced it in my own docstring.

title: has_fallback_tier was added with the ladder and had zero production callers
rule_violated: A remediation branch must not add controls that are written, exported, unit-tested and never called -- that is the defect class it exists to delete.
notes: Found by the audit's regression hunter, which was asked to locate a production callsite for each of the ten symbols this branch introduced. has_fallback_tier had none: run_with_model_fallback does its own MODEL_FALLBACK_TIER.get(model) because it needs the TARGET tier rather than a boolean, and the only other reference was the test asserting the topology. Speculative API in the one branch whose whole purpose is removing unreachable controls. Removed rather than given a synthetic caller; the test now reads MODEL_FALLBACK_TIER directly, which is the SSoT anyway. A comment marks the spot so the next author does not re-add it.

title: Cost rows recorded at exactly a window boundary were dropped, under-counting spend against a safety cap
rule_violated: Timestamps must be compared as instants. Two ISO spellings of the same moment sort differently as strings.
notes: read_cost_attribution filtered with a raw string comparison recorded_at < since_iso. Rows are written by utc_now() as 2026-07-28T00:00:00+00:00 while callers build windows as 2026-07-28T00:00:00Z. Through the seconds the strings are identical, then '+' (0x2B) sorts below 'Z' (0x5A), so a row recorded at EXACTLY the window start compared as earlier than the window and was skipped -- one row per day boundary and one per month boundary silently absent from derived_usage. The direction matters: it UNDER-counts, so a cost cap binds later than the operator configured. Fixed by comparing parsed instants in _before_instant, which removes the class rather than making two spellings agree by convention, and normalises Z, +00:00 and naive forms. Unparseable input is treated as NOT-before so a malformed row inflates a budget rather than vanishing from it.

title: The 72h failure window that fixed ORPHAN-MEDIUM-468 was itself the boundary value, so the bleed case still coin-flipped at the enforcement gate
rule_violated: A window must exceed threshold x cadence, not merely cadence; and a test must evaluate at the gate that reads the value, not at the instant it is written.
notes: Found by the audit. My fix for 468 replaced a hardcoded 24 with a hardcoded 72 and pinned the invariant at window > 24 -- i.e. window > CADENCE. The correct relationship is window > threshold x cadence. Walk it: failures land at t=0/24/48, but the breaker is not read at the trip instant, it is read at the NEXT night's preflight, t=72, where a 72h window spans exactly [0, 72] and the oldest failure sits precisely on the edge. Thirty minutes of cron jitter therefore includes or excludes it and the verdict flips between blocked and ok -- the original 468 defect, one boundary further out. My multi-night test could not see it because it counted at t=48 rather than at the gate. Closed by DERIVING the window as threshold x cadence + cadence (96h at threshold 3), clamping any narrower operator override up to that floor, and asserting the RELATIONSHIP in the invariant instead of a magic number. The derivation lives in genesis_policy because the value existed as two independent literals -- CIRCUIT_BREAKER_DEFAULTS carried its own 72 and circuit_breaker carried another; circuit_breaker imports genesis_policy, so the lower module owns it. A negative control pins that the old 72h window loses a failure at the gate, and it earned its place: the first version of the new test passed age_hours keys where the helper reads a ts timestamp, so every row was unparseable and counted via the ORPHAN-CRITICAL-418 fail-closed rule -- the test asserted nothing until the control exposed it.

title: The executor could publish a queue-less bootstrapped tree under the canonical aria-tools-state name, burying the producer's queue with no automated recovery
rule_violated: A gate that overwrites another writer's state must require positive proof of ancestry, not merely that the state it holds looks internally consistent.
notes: Introduced by the S1 queue-bridge fix (ORPHAN-CRITICAL-469) and found by the adversarial audit. The publish gate was `state_valid == 'true'`, and the integrity verifier reports valid for a freshly BOOTSTRAPPED tree. On a run where the restore does not happen, actions/checkout still materialises the 10 git-tracked aria-tools files, and the steps that run BEFORE the verify step -- `agent next-pending` at :319 and the two `handoff snapshot` calls at :331/:415 -- create the missing integrity_index.json. So by the time the gate is evaluated the tree looks healthy and a queue-less tree is published under the canonical name with `overwrite: true`, burying the producer's queue. The failure is ABSORBING: each such night buries the good artifact one run deeper until the 30-day retention window closes. THE VERDICT HISTORY IS THE INSTRUCTIVE PART. Two auditors disagreed and the first refutation was confidently wrong: it ran `integrity verify` on the checkout-only tree IN ISOLATION, measured exit 1 with bootstrap_incomplete, and concluded the gate fails closed. That is a real measurement of the wrong state -- the intervening steps have already indexed the tree by the time the gate reads it. A second investigator reproduced the true state by replaying the executor's own step sequence and got status=ok valid=True exit 0. Verifying a step in isolation is not verifying the job, and a high-confidence measurement of the wrong precondition is more dangerous than no measurement. Closed by recording positive ancestry proof (`restored=true`) at the only place that knows it -- the restore step's success path -- and making it a precondition of the canonical publish. Only the TRUE case is ever written, so absence blocks: the no-artifact fail-open branch, a step failure, a skipped step and a crash all leave the output unset. The quarantine step now also catches `restored != true` (with `overwrite: true`, since github.run_id repeats across re-run attempts and a re-attempted upload would 409), and a final fail step makes a blocked publish RED rather than silently green -- mirroring the sibling producer, whose equivalent step had not been copied to the consumer.

title: The failure breaker's producer was unreachable on the scheduled lane at four independent levels, and its end-to-end test could not see any of them
rule_violated: A producer must be placed on a path a schedule actually walks under the profile that schedule uses. A test that calls a private function with a synthetic error proves the function works, not that anything reaches it.
notes: The S5 commit claimed the producer sat 'on a path proven reachable from a schedule (aria-auto-cycle.yml -> autonomy run -> run_enterprise_cycle -> _run_extended_phases -> _run_pr_lifecycle_phase)'. The audit falsified that chain at four independent levels: (1) _run_extended_phases only executes when run_phases is not None, and the autonomy orchestrator calls cycle_runner with four kwargs and no run_phases -- verified by running the real run_enterprise_cycle with the orchestrator's exact kwargs and a spy on the phase: zero invocations, extended_phases {}; (2) the callsite is gated on pr_create, which the nightly's `standard` profile does NOT permit, so enforce_profile_for_action raises profile_violation at pr_manager.py:155, ninety-two lines before the perimeter check at :247, and the message therefore never carries PERIMETER_REFUSED_PREFIX -- verified: 5 refusals, sliding_count 0; (3) the proposal set it iterates has no autonomous producer (approve_proposal has zero non-test callers); (4) it consequently recorded nothing on any schedule. The reachability claim was reused from a verification done for a DIFFERENT finding and never re-established for this path. The new test could not see any of it because it called the private _run_pr_lifecycle_phase directly and injected a synthetic perimeter GovernanceError -- verbatim the defect class this branch exists to close, reproduced by the remediation. Closed by moving the producer to the planner dispatch hook's subprocess-timeout arm, which the nightly genuinely reaches: aria-auto-cycle.yml -> `autonomy run --profile standard` -> run_autonomy_orchestrator calls the planner drainer unconditionally after the cycle phase, the drainer's default hook is that function, and its profile gate is agent_claim, which `standard` permits. It records kind=subprocess_timeout, already a declared FAILURE_KIND and literally what happened; the discrimination is STRUCTURAL -- only that except arm records -- rather than a prefix match on an error message, so it cannot drift the way PERIMETER_REFUSED_PREFIX did. The ledger write is wrapped so a breaker-ledger failure cannot convert a dispatch timeout into a crash or lose the governance event written before it. The pr_lifecycle callsite stays wired for the operator-driven strict/autonomous lane. The replacement test drives the PUBLIC dispatch_one_pending_planner_request entry point with only the subprocess boundary mocked, asserts a row lands in the real breaker ledger, and was verified to FAIL (0 != 1) with the producer deleted.

title: ARIA can open an unbounded PR: plan_pr_split exists but no autonomous path calls it, so nothing caps what the implementer submits
rule_violated: Operator rule (2026-07-28): an ARIA-authored PR must not be large. A size bound that is available but never consulted is not a bound.
notes: Operator requirement, to be implemented in a FOLLOW-UP PR after the current branch merges (explicit instruction). Verified gap, not an assumption: plan_pr_split(max_files_per_pr=12) exists at pr_manager.py:531, but `grep -rn 'plan_pr_split('` returns exactly two callers -- cli.py:3428 (an operator-invoked command) and one test. The autonomous PR-open path never consults it, so aria-implementer can submit a PR of any size. Same defect class as the rest of this branch: the control is written, defaulted, tested, and unreachable from the path that matters. PROPOSED SHAPE (needs operator sign-off on the numbers before implementation): add a pr_size_within_bounds check to the PRE-PR-OPEN stage of implementation_safety.HARD_FAIL_CHECKS -- the stage that already refuses a non-compliant submission -- so an oversized PR is REFUSED rather than opened and then complained about. Bound on BOTH changed-file count and added-line count, because a 3-file 4000-line diff is exactly as unreviewable as a 40-file one and the existing helper only counts files. On refusal the implementer should be handed the plan_pr_split grouping so the work is split rather than abandoned, which is what makes this a bound rather than a dead end. OPEN DECISION for the operator: the file cap (existing default 12) and a line cap (no current value anywhere in the repo). Generated files and lockfiles need an exemption list or a single formatting commit will trip it.

title: Nothing stops ARIA promoting a second plan while one is still in flight, so it can leave half-finished work behind
rule_violated: Operator rule (2026-07-28): ARIA must not start a new plan before the current one is completely finished, and must not leave work half-done.
notes: Operator requirement, to be implemented in a FOLLOW-UP PR after the current branch merges (explicit instruction). Verified gap: list_active_plans() exists at plan_convergence.py:573 and correctly derives the in-flight set from the event log, but promote_converged_plan_to_dispatch() at promotion_controller.py:16 never calls it. `grep -rn 'list_active_plans'` finds exactly one consumer, learning.py:179, which merely REPORTS the list in a cycle summary. So the data needed to enforce single-plan-at-a-time is computed, cached and published, and no gate reads it -- again the same class. PROPOSED SHAPE (two halves, both needed; the first without the second would merely block forever): (1) ADMISSION -- promote_converged_plan_to_dispatch refuses when list_active_plans() is non-empty and the candidate is not that plan, emitting a governance row naming the blocking plan_id, so concurrency becomes structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged. (2) COMPLETION -- define terminal precisely, because 'finished' is the load-bearing word in the operator's rule and the state machine's IMPLEMENTATION_IN_FLIGHT (plan_convergence.py:41) has no explicit exit. A plan is finished only when every key_change is applied AND its PR is merged or closed; a plan whose PR is open is still in flight, which is what prevents the half-done case the operator is guarding against. Needs a reaper for the failure mode this creates: a plan whose PR is abandoned would block ARIA forever, so there must be a timeout or an operator-invoked release, with the release recorded in governance. OPEN DECISION for the operator: how long an in-flight plan may block before it is auto-released, and whether a closed-unmerged PR counts as finished (work abandoned) or as failed (needs rework).

title: The ORPHAN-CRITICAL-484 ancestry gate made a first-ever ARIA run impossible: a newborn tree could never publish, permanently
rule_violated: A gate that requires proof of ancestry must distinguish 'no ancestor exists yet' from 'the ancestor could not be reached'. Collapsing them makes bootstrap impossible.
notes: Self-inflicted by the ORPHAN-CRITICAL-484 fix and exposed by the operator's decision to reset ARIA and start it as if newborn. 484 closed a real hole -- a bootstrapped tree passing the integrity gate and being published under the canonical name, burying the producer's queue -- by requiring positive ancestry proof (restored=true) written only on the restore step's success path, with absence blocking. The design note said explicitly: 'only the TRUE case is ever written, so absence blocks: the no-artifact fail-open branch, a step failure, a skipped step and a crash all leave it unset.' Listing the no-artifact branch alongside the failure cases WAS the defect, stated in my own comment and not noticed. On a genuine first run there is no prior artifact, so the restore takes its SystemExit(0) branch, writes nothing, the publish is gated off, and the new 'Fail when aria-tools state was not published' step turns the job RED. Permanently: with nothing published, the next run is also a first run. ARIA could never establish its initial artifact. This did not fire earlier only because artifact 8396940432 stayed live until 2026-08-16, which the audit noted -- so the trap was latent behind a 30-day retention window and would have detonated on any deliberate reset or any expiry. Closed by distinguishing THREE states at the only step that can tell them apart: bootstrap=true on the no-live-artifact branch (written BEFORE the clean exit, and before any extraction), restored=true after a real extraction, and NEITHER on failure, skip or crash. The publish permits restored OR bootstrap; quarantine and the fail step take the exact inverse, so no state satisfies both gates or neither. Pinned by tests asserting the three-way split and that bootstrap is claimed only on the no-artifact path; verified by removing the bootstrap conjunct, which fails two of them.

title: ClaudeCreditExhausted escaped ci_executor.main() uncaught, leaking the claim for the full lease window
rule_violated: A raise added to close a fail-open path must land in a handler that releases in-flight state. An exception with no handler converts a silent wrong answer into a silent resource leak.
notes: Found by the S2 review panel while attacking a DIFFERENT fix, which is the whole argument for reviewing with many hands: the writer was looking at ResourceLimitsUnavailable and this sibling raise was invisible from that vantage point. I introduced ClaudeCreditExhausted in ORPHAN-HIGH-475 so a CLI usage-limit notice could not be returned as the agent's answer, and then left it out of every except tuple -- grep confirmed zero occurrences in either executor. So a quota-exhausted run escaped main() with the claim still CLAIMED, blocking that request for the full lease window; a billing event, which is the most likely reason to exhaust credit mid-cycle, would therefore also stall the queue. Exactly the ResourceLimitsUnavailable defect one release earlier, committed in the code that fixed the previous instance. Closed by adding it to the arm that already lands every refused spawn and releases the claim with reason=claude_spawn_refused. Two secondary corrections in the same commit: the arm's comment claimed 'every other fail-fast branch in main() releases', which a reviewer flagged as unverified -- narrowed to the two branches actually checked rather than left as a claim nobody had tested. And the first version of the regression test sliced the handler body at the literal 'return 1', which appears inside the arm's OWN comment ('It used to `return 1` with the claim still CLAIMED'), truncating the body before the assertion target; that is the FOURTH test this session to match prose instead of code, so the slice is now structural, by indentation, which cannot match a comment.

title: The workflow abort gate matched its guard by substring, so an ||-joined always() disjunct passed as guarded
rule_violated: A safety gate must reject every expression that does not actually gate. Substring containment is not evaluation.
notes: _verify_abort_gate (workflow_contracts.py:450) decides a post-gate step is guarded with `if guard in condition or announce in condition: continue` at :481. _collapse (:376) only strips whitespace, so this is raw substring containment against the step's `if:` text. A step written `if: ${{ <guard> || always() }}` CONTAINS the guard verbatim and is therefore waved through, while the always() disjunct makes the condition unconditionally true -- the step runs during a blocked cycle. That is precisely the failure the gate's own docstring at :459 says it exists to prevent: in aria-agent-executor it meant claiming a request and invoking an agent while another host held the autonomous-loop lease. The same hole admits any widening disjunct (`|| github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'`, `|| success()`), and admits a guard appearing inside a string literal or a comment-like fragment. FIX (tier 1 -- make the wrong shape unrepresentable rather than merely detected): strip the ${{ }} wrapper, split the collapsed condition on TOP-LEVEL || only (parenthesis-depth aware, so nested disjunctions inside a conjunct are not mistaken for top-level branches), and require EVERY resulting disjunct to contain the guard or the announce expression. `A || always()` is then rejected because the always() branch carries neither, while `(guard && x) || (guard && y)` still passes. The second half matters as much as the first: _collapse's own docstring records that an over-strict gate 'would get deleted for being noisy', so the fix must be proven to reject the inert form WITHOUT rejecting correctly-guarded fan-out, and the regression test asserts both directions.

title: next_pending_request never read the target_sha it selects on, so a request minted against an obsolete tree stayed claimable forever
rule_violated: A request must not be executed against a tree it does not describe. Selection is the last point at which the repo is still in scope.
notes: Same defect class as the rest of this branch, and the sharpest instance of it yet: the control was not merely uncalled, it was fully MINTED. target_sha is written onto every request row (agent_invocations.py:519), threaded from convergence_drainer.py:575 via _resolve_workspace_head_sha -- documented there as 'the commit SHA the plan's evidence is grounded at' -- and hashed into the context envelope at :128. The evidence-validator reads it to grade refs as repo_verified. The SELECTION path, next_pending_request:1183, ignored it entirely and returned the oldest PENDING row whatever the repo had done since. NOT HYPOTHETICAL: ORPHAN-CRITICAL-469 stranded ~20 requests in the live aria-tools-state artifact, minted before 2026-07-17 against a tree now 60+ commits back; with the queue bridge repaired the first executor run would have claimed one and dispatched an agent against a plan that no longer describes the repo. WHY AGE AND NOT JUST REACHABILITY: those stranded anchors ARE ancestors of HEAD -- same branch lineage -- so an existence check alone passes every one of them. Both tests are needed and both are applied. FIX: (1) new terminal derived state ANCHOR_STALE, deliberately NOT folded into STALE, because STALE is lease expiry and is retryable whereas an obsolete anchor cannot be made current by retrying; (2) the git evaluation runs at the selection boundary and its outcome is appended ONCE as a terminal claims-ledger event, which keeps derive_request_state a pure function over ledgers (its documented contract -- two callers on different checkouts must derive the same state from the same files) while the repo-dependent decision happens where the repo is in scope; (3) the window is genesis-policy config (agent_request_anchor.max_age_seconds, default 3d) rather than a constant, because the right window follows the cycle cadence and an operator changing the cadence must not need a code change. The one-off reset of the 20 live rows is DERIVED from this rule rather than performed as an operator ceremony -- they carry no anchor and are refused automatically, so there is nothing to remember to do. Enforcement engages only where a git work tree actually contains the tools dir (production layout), so an isolated fixture with no repo has nothing to be stale against and queue semantics are unchanged.

title: reserve_cycle_budget remains an orphaned USD enforcement point after the dispatch gate moved to wall clock
rule_violated: A control that is exported, tested and called from nowhere reads as protection that does not exist. Partial consolidation must be declared, not implied.
notes: DECLARED INCOMPLETE WORK, raised by me against my own change rather than left implicit. The ORPHAN-HIGH-472 fix moved the executor's dispatch gate from estimated USD to per-cycle wall clock and deleted the two dead USD helpers in ci_executor (_max_budget_usd, _max_budget_usd_per_cycle, _estimate_envelope_cost_usd). The approved plan ALSO said reserve_cycle_budget -- the third orphaned cost-enforcement point -- would be consolidated into the same accounting in that commit. IT WAS NOT, and the commit says so. WHY NOT: reserve_cycle_budget is pinned by v8 prerequisite invariants (test_phase_v8_0_prerequisites.py:172-212) and its --max-budget-usd-per-run / --max-budget-usd-per-cycle CLI flags are pinned by test_phase_v9_7_cli_flags.py:41. Removing or repurposing it means editing pinned invariants late in a 65-commit PR that is currently green, which is exactly the trade the PR-size guardrail (ORPHAN-HIGH-486) exists to discourage. Shipping it half-done and calling 472 fully closed would have been the worse option. CURRENT STATE, precisely: reserve_cycle_budget still exists, still reads MAX_BUDGET_USD_PER_RUN / MAX_BUDGET_USD_PER_CYCLE, and still has NO production callers -- the two workflow flags that used to set those env vars were removed from aria-auto-cycle.yml because they contradicted each other ($20.00/run against $3.00/cycle in the same invocation). So it is now an orphan whose inputs are also unset: harmless today, misleading to the next reader. WHAT CLOSING IT LOOKS LIKE: either delete it and its CLI flags outright (the honest option, since under a subscription session there is no per-run charge for it to reserve against), or convert it into the wall-clock reservation the orchestrator lane needs -- note autonomy_orchestrator already has cycle_deadline_seconds, but checks it AFTER each cycle completes rather than before starting work, so the producer lane has the same never-start-what-cannot-finish gap the executor lane just closed. The second option is the larger and better one.

title: The ORPHAN-MEDIUM-492 anchor guard read absence-in-a-shallow-clone as proof of unreachability, terminally killing every cross-run request
rule_violated: A fail-closed guard must distinguish a fact from a guess. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, and a terminal state may not be entered on an indeterminate reading.
notes: SELF-INFLICTED, caught before it ever ran, and strictly worse than the defect it was introduced to fix. My ORPHAN-MEDIUM-492 fix refused a request whose target_sha failed `git cat-file -e` as anchor_unreachable, and recorded that refusal as the TERMINAL state ANCHOR_STALE. Neither ARIA lane sets fetch-depth on actions/checkout (aria-agent-executor.yml:58, aria-auto-cycle.yml:92), so both run on the default depth-1 SHALLOW clone holding only the tip commit. Therefore a request minted by the 01:00 producer and consumed by the 02:00 executor -- the entire point of the queue bridge, and the thing ORPHAN-CRITICAL-469 was raised to repair -- has an anchor that is simply ABSENT from the consumer's clone the moment any commit has landed in between. The guard would have read that absence as unreachable and killed the request permanently: not deferred, not requeued, terminal. Net effect would have been an ARIA that silently discards its own queue on the first live night, with a governance row that reads like correct enforcement. That is the fail-open-to-fail-closed regression class in its most dangerous form -- a guard that halts everything while reporting that it is working. FIX: reachability is now consulted only when the repo is NOT shallow (`git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`). On a shallow checkout the reachability question is indeterminate and is not used to refuse; the age check needs no history and still fires, so the stale-queue case 492 exists to catch is still caught on exactly the checkout production uses -- both directions are pinned by tests (test_shallow_clone_does_not_kill_a_cross_run_request, test_shallow_clone_still_refuses_an_aged_request). Reverting the shallow guard fails the first with 'a cross-run request must survive a shallow checkout'. HOW IT WAS FOUND: I raised it against myself while scoping the regression review lens, by asking what the guard does under the checkout production actually uses rather than the one the fixture used. The fixture was a full local clone, which is why seven passing tests said nothing about it -- the same fixture-does-not-match-production blindness that let the original 492 defect survive. WORTH NOTING for the next reader: the alternative fix (fetch-depth: 0 on both lanes) was rejected because a full-history clone every run is a real cost paid nightly to answer a question that only matters on the rare force-push, and it would have made the guard's correctness depend on a workflow setting far from the code that relies on it.

title: The anchor guard killed every unanchored request terminally, and the wall-clock gate it shipped beside was inert on 15 of 17 mint paths
rule_violated: A guard may not enter a terminal state on absence of evidence, and a gate that cannot fire is not a gate.
notes: TWO self-inflicted defects in the same closeout, found by the regression review lens and confirmed by direct AST count of all 17 create_agent_invocation_request callsites. (A) ANCHOR_MISSING WAS TERMINAL. Only 6 of 17 mint paths pass target_sha. The other 11 -- cli.py:2951 (the operator's own `aria-kernel agent request`), human_required_adjudication.py:226 (THIS BRANCH's new HUMAN_REQUIRED panel, so it could never have been dispatched), review_runner.py:266, specialist_review_runner.py:476, plan_round_controller.py:102+154, dispatcher_factory.py:156+208, autonomy_orchestrator.py:220, cross_review_bridge.py:468 -- would every one have been marked terminally ANCHOR_STALE on first selection, with no requeue path in the CLI. A guard written to protect the queue would have destroyed it. FIX: a missing anchor is no longer grounds for refusal; the age check does the real work and needs no anchor, because created_at is on every row. The stranded pre-07-17 requests are therefore still cleared, anchored or not. (B) THE WALL-CLOCK GATE WAS INERT. The ORPHAN-HIGH-472 gate accounted against request['cycle_id'], and 15 of 17 mint paths never set it, so _assert_cycle_wall_clock returned early on essentially every dispatch: written, unit-tested, name-pinned, and unreachable in production -- precisely the defect class this whole branch exists to close, committed by me in the commit that claimed to close it. FIX: the ceiling now derives from GITHUB_RUN_STARTED_AT, i.e. elapsed job time, which needs nothing threaded through the envelope. That is also the better question for this lane: the executor handles ONE request per job, so there is no cycle total to accumulate; what matters is whether a 30-minute run still fits in what remains of a 35-minute job after restore, preflight and lease checks have taken their share. Per-cycle accounting is retained for telemetry only. LESSON, and the reason both survived my own review: every test I wrote constructed its own request with the field present. Neither fixture resembled the 11 production callsites that omit it. Same fixture-does-not-match-production blindness as ORPHAN-CRITICAL-494, three times in one session.

title: Two hand-maintained copies of the non-delivering terminal-state set fell behind the SSoT when ANCHOR_STALE was added
rule_violated: A derived set must be derived. Two hand-maintained copies of one list is a drift generator, not a definition.
notes: Found by the regression review lens. review_runner.py:81 and specialist_review_runner.py:61 each carried a literal frozenset of the terminal states that can never yield an accepted result. Adding ANCHOR_STALE to agent_surface.TERMINAL_REQUEST_STATES (ORPHAN-MEDIUM-492) updated neither copy, so an anchor-refused request was terminal-but-unrecognised: the poll loop would burn its full judge_timeout_seconds / specialist_timeout_seconds waiting for a result that could not arrive -- turning a fast fail into a slow one on the very lane that had just gained a wall-clock ceiling, so the two defects compounded. FIX: both are now DERIVED as TERMINAL_REQUEST_STATES - {'ACCEPTED'}. Every terminal state except ACCEPTED is non-delivering by definition, so the single exception is what gets named and any future terminal state joins both consumers automatically. ACCEPTED stays excluded deliberately -- that path is detected by the presence of the accepted result row itself, not by the state string, so a state claiming ACCEPTED without a readable result row still fails closed. This is tier 2 of the hierarchy (make the correct behaviour the zero-effort default) replacing what was effectively tier 4 (two comments asking future readers to remember).

title: The wall-clock gate refused every dispatch under production values, and the abort gate accepted an inverted guard on any step
rule_violated: A gate must be tested with the values production supplies. A test parameterised away from production proves nothing about production.
notes: Both found by the TEST-QUALITY review lens, which executed the code rather than reading it. (A) THE GATE REFUSED EVERYTHING. Cap was (35 - 5) * 60 = 1800s and the executor workflow sets MAX_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=1800, so `remaining < per_run_timeout` was false ONLY at elapsed == 0. Measured: 5s in -> REFUSED, 30s in -> REFUSED, 300s in -> REFUSED. main() catches WallClockExhausted, releases the claim and returns 0 -- so the executor lane would have become permanently green-and-idle: claim, refuse, release, exit 0, forever, with no agent ever running, no job red, and no breaker row. My three tests all passed timeout_seconds=600, a value _max_timeout_seconds() cannot return on either lane; the test named test_fresh_job_has_room_for_a_dispatch is exactly the one that should have caught it and was parameterised away from production. FIX: the gate also revealed a REAL latent config problem rather than only my arithmetic -- an 1800s run does not fit a 2100s job once startup and publish are counted -- so the executor job timeout moves 35 -> 45 minutes (contract pinned in lockstep, _verify_job_timeout_minutes rejects drift) and the tests now READ cap and per-run timeout from their sources, asserting cap - startup > per_run so any future retune that makes the gate unsatisfiable fails there. (B) INVERTED GUARD ACCEPTED ANYWHERE. _step_is_gated exempted the announce expression globally rather than on the declared announce step, so flipping one character on a worker step (`!=` to `==`) made the CI executor run ONLY while another host held the autonomous-loop lease -- claiming requests and dispatching agents against a tree being mutated elsewhere, i.e. ORPHAN-CRITICAL-469 restored with the contract gate green. Measured: inverted guard on 'Run CI executor' gave valid=True. FIX: WorkflowAbortGate gains announce_step; the exemption is scoped to it; the inversion mutation is now in the abort-gate battery alongside removal, wrong-output and ||-widening. Re-globalising the exemption fails the new test. PATTERN, fourth instance this session: every one of these survived because the fixture did not resemble production -- a full clone where production is shallow (494), a request dict with fields 11 mint paths omit (495), a timeout literal production never emits (this one). The lens that caught it ran the code; the lenses that missed it read it.

title: The pre-PR-open perimeter is not on the scheduled lane: _run_extended_phases is entered by no production caller, so ORPHAN-CRITICAL-428 is operator-path only
rule_violated: Optional safety is not safety. A safety-critical phase may not be gated on an optional keyword argument that no production caller supplies.
notes: SUCCESSOR to ORPHAN-CRITICAL-428, raised because 428's closure claim is narrower than it reads and the registry is append-only (a new row is the only honest correction mechanism -- history is not rewritten). HOW IT WAS FOUND: the two review lenses CONTRADICTED each other. The regression lens predicted the perimeter would trip the breaker on the nightly lane; the test-quality lens said that path is unreachable. Resolved against the source: `grep` for `run_phases=` / `pre_tool_phases=` across aria-kernel/, tools/ and .github/ returns ONE COMMENT AND NO CALLER. CHAIN: _run_extended_phases (cycle.py:704) is entered only when a caller passes run_phases or pre_tool_phases -> nobody does -> _run_pr_lifecycle_phase (cycle.py:868) never executes -> its open_pr_for_action(dry_run=True) call at cycle.py:897 never executes -> run_hard_fail_checks, whose ONLY caller is pr_manager.py:247 inside open_pr_for_action, runs in production ONLY via cli.py:3403 (the operator typing `pr open`). So the pre-PR-open perimeter that 428 exists to wire has never executed on the scheduled/autonomous lane. TWO CONSEQUENCES, both recorded rather than implied: (1) PR #1024's S9 row and its 428 line overstate reach and are corrected in the PR body and in the test file's own docstrings, which asserted the dead route as production fact -- precisely what let this survive review; (2) the regression lens's self-halt HIGH is REFUTED on reachability (the perimeter cannot trip the breaker because it does not run), and is replaced by this worse finding: not 'the perimeter halts the lane' but 'the perimeter is not on the lane'. ALSO DEAD on the same path: record_failure at cycle.py:948 -- but the breaker producer survives via planner_dispatch_hook.py:388 (reached through convergence_drainer.py:83), so ORPHAN-CRITICAL-485 IS genuinely closed. sweep_human_required_adjudications is live (run_enterprise_cycle, cycle.py:503); only its test is blind (ORPHAN-HIGH-499). FIX, tracked as RC-1 of the follow-up plan and NOT attempted in this PR: collapse the two cycle pipelines into one declarative CYCLE_PHASES registry whose preconditions are an enumerated set, DELETE run_phases/pre_tool_phases rather than keep a compatibility seam (a second entrance to the same phases is the cause), and add a static call-graph reachability invariant asserting every declared safety control is reachable from a production entry point. That invariant is the generalised answer to this defect class and would have caught 494, 495, 497 and both lens CRITICALs without a review cycle -- grep is what said 428 was wired.

title: test_human_required_adjudication_sweep asserts an import, not a call: deleting the production call leaves the entire 2943-test suite byte-identical
rule_violated: A wiring test must fail when the wiring is removed. Asserting a symbol is importable proves nothing about whether it is invoked.
notes: Found by the TEST-QUALITY review lens and PROVEN BY MUTATION, not argued. test_human_required_adjudication_sweep.py:56-72 asserts hasattr(cycle, 'sweep_human_required_adjudications') and the identity of the imported symbol -- an import, not a call -- while its own docstring claims it 'survives any refactor that keeps the call and fails on any refactor that drops it'. The sibling at :74-94 asserts only that some dict literal in cycle.py carries the key 'human_required_adjudication', which a constant satisfies. MUTATION RESULT: replacing the call at cycle.py:503 with `human_required_adjudication = {"status": "ok"}` (call deleted, import retained) leaves all 6 tests in the file green AND the entire 2943-test kernel suite BYTE-IDENTICAL to baseline -- zero delta. No Python linter runs in CI (.github/workflows/aria-kernel*.yml execute only `python3 -m unittest discover`), so the now-orphaned import is not flagged either. CONSEQUENCE: ORPHAN-HIGH-426's HUMAN_REQUIRED adjudication panel can go dead a second time -- escalations raised every cycle and cleared by nobody -- with a green suite and a green test whose name asserts the panel has a caller. IMPORTANT DISTINCTION from ORPHAN-CRITICAL-498: the sweep call itself IS live, inside run_enterprise_cycle (cycle.py:503, which is the real cycle body, not the dead _run_extended_phases branch). So this is purely a blind-test defect, not a dead-path defect, and the two must not be conflated. FIX: patch the symbol and assert invocation, reusing the pattern already CORRECT in this repo at test_pr_open_perimeter_callsite.py:132-142 (patch where the module looked the name up, then assert_called_once). Not a new mechanism -- the right shape already exists here and the defect is that this file did not use it. Tracked as RC-7 of the follow-up plan.

title: The pre-commit hook mirrors only one of CI's two format gates: `format check-changed` has no local counterpart, so eight commits shipped Prettier drift before CI objected
rule_violated: A gate that blocks merge in CI must have a local counterpart that fires earlier, or the local mirror is a false assurance. Mirroring one of a pair and claiming the pair is covered is worse than mirroring neither, because the developer stops looking.
notes: FOUND BY CI, not by review -- which is itself the point. PR #1024's first real CI run (30495813228, head 300526134) went red on `lint-and-typecheck` step 10, `quality.mjs format check-changed`, with ten Prettier-drifted files, every one of them authored in this session: docs/plans/2026-06-18-enterprise-grade-debt-closure/finding-truth-table.md, docs/plans/2026-07-26-aria-software-team-program/PLAN.md, docs/reviews/2026-07-26-aria-codex-audit-verification.md, tests/invariants/workflow-npm-script-references.spec.ts, and six tools/gates files (aria-authority-hash.ts, commit-msg-validator.ts, finding-registry.ts, finding-registry-store.ts, finding-registry-store.spec.ts, repin-debt-plan.ts). ROOT CAUSE: CI runs TWO format gates -- `format-scope check` (manifest freshness) and `format check-changed` (actual drift) -- and .husky/pre-commit runs only the first. The hook's own comment states the intent exactly: 'Push sonrasi CI kirmizisi yerine commit aninda yakala (tier-3 make-it-detectable)'. So the intent was written down and half-implemented; the gate that catches drift has no local counterpart at all. MEASURED CONSEQUENCE: eight commits on this branch shipped drift with a green pre-commit hook every time. This is the SAME DEFECT CLASS the branch exists to close (ORPHAN-HIGH-455: a control written, tested, exported, and not wired where it matters) in mirror image -- here the CI side is wired and the local mirror is the half that is missing. SECOND-ORDER DEFECT: quality.mjs offers modes `check | check-changed | write` and no `write-changed`, so the only one-command fix a developer can reach for is repo-wide `format write`, which rewrites every managed file including the ~28 that check-changed deliberately quarantines as pre-existing base debt -- burying a 10-file fix in 38 files of churn. The missing write mode is why the drift was tedious to fix correctly and therefore likely to be fixed incorrectly. FIX (tier 2 + tier 3): extract the regression-set computation out of runPrettierChanged into a shared computeFormatRegressions(base); add a `write-changed` mode over exactly that set; add a staged-mode drift check to .husky/pre-commit (staged, not the HEAD^ fallback, because at pre-commit time the content under test is uncommitted so HEAD^ is the wrong base); and pin the mirror with an invariant asserting every quality.mjs gate in ci-full.yml's lint-and-typecheck job has a pre-commit counterpart or a stated exemption. Without the last part this is a one-time repair of a recurring class. NOTE ON BLAST RADIUS, verified not assumed: reformatting these ten files does not move the ARIA authority hash -- AUTHORITY_ROOTS is ['docs/aria','aria-kernel','tools/aria-poc'] (aria-authority-hash.ts:67) and none of the ten fall under it; and repin-debt-plan.ts anchors are fail-closed via substituteOrThrow (:112), so a moved anchor fails loudly rather than corrupting a mirror.

title: lint-and-typecheck exceeds its 15-minute budget after the merge, so the job is cancelled before its last two gates run — the format check has not executed in CI-Full on any recent head
rule_violated: A gate job's time budget must exceed its measured workload with headroom. When it does not, the job is cancelled at whatever step it reached and every later step reports `skipped` — the gates at the tail of the job stop running while the job still looks like a configured gate.
notes: MEASURED, not inferred. ci-full.yml:39 sets `timeout-minutes: 15` on lint-and-typecheck. On head 5967d7285 (run 30520580511) the job started 06:45:42 and was cancelled 07:00:55 — 15m13s — inside step 9 `Run type-check-spec gate`, with step 10 `Check formatting of changed files` reported `skipped`. No push followed 5967d7285, so this was the job timeout and not the concurrency cancel-in-progress that killed the previous run. Step timings: linter 8m57s (06:47:02-06:55:59), type check 3m8s (06:55:59-06:59:07), plus ~1.3m setup/install/rust. type-check-spec needs ~1.9m (measured 06:31:11-06:33:08 on run 30495813228) and the format check ~16s, so the job needs ~17.5m against a 15m budget. WHY IT CHANGED: on head 300526134 the same job completed in 12m25s with the linter taking 6m36s. The merge of main added the @aquaculture/testing workspace, so `nx run-many --target=lint` covers more projects and the linter grew to 8m57s, tipping the job over its limit. CONSEQUENCE, and it is the part that matters: a cancelled job runs none of its remaining steps, so BOTH tail gates silently stop executing. `Check formatting of changed files` shows `skipped` on runs 30520045513 and 30520580511 — the gate whose absence from the pre-commit hook is ORPHAN-HIGH-500 is now also not running in CI, one layer up. The safety property still holds (build-status treats cancelled as not-success and fails closed, so nothing merges), but the diagnosis is actively misleading: build-status prints `Lint/Typecheck failed`, which sends the reader to look for a lint error that does not exist. FIX: raise the budget to fit the measured workload with headroom, consistent with the file's own conventions (test 30, build 30, deploy-ssot-gates 20). NOT FIXED HERE, and deliberately separated: the job does four heavy serial passes (lint all, tsc all, a second full tsc pass in type-check-spec, format) and splitting them into parallel jobs would be the better design, but the job names are wired into the `build-status` aggregate and into the required-status-check manifest, so renaming or splitting them touches branch protection and belongs in its own change with the ruleset updated in lockstep.

title: The dead pr_lifecycle route was still asserted as production fact in two places the ORPHAN-CRITICAL-498 correction missed: a superseded invariant named ..._end_to_end_reachability and a load-bearing comment in pr_manager.py
rule_violated: A comment or test name asserting a code path is the production route is a claim, and a false one is worse than none: it is what a future reader or agent greps before concluding a control is wired. When a reachability finding is corrected, every artifact repeating the refuted claim must be corrected with it, not only the one the reviewer happened to open.
notes: ORPHAN-CRITICAL-498 established that `_run_extended_phases` has no production caller, so `_run_pr_lifecycle_phase` never executes and the pre-PR-open perimeter runs only when an operator types `pr open`. That correction was applied to test_pr_open_perimeter_callsite.py's docstring and MISSED two other artifacts making the same refuted claim. (1) tests/invariants/v3/test_breaker_end_to_end_reachability.py claimed to run 'the REAL chain' while calling cycle_mod._run_pr_lifecycle_phase directly at lines 79 and 121 — a green invariant whose NAME is exactly what someone greps for before shipping a lane with no producer. Its successor already existed (test_breaker_producer_scheduled_lane.py) with a header enumerating four ways the old path was dead, and the old file was neither deleted nor annotated: two files claiming one invariant. (2) pr_manager.py carried, in the load-bearing comment justifying where the perimeter check sits, the assertion that 'the only production route into this function today is the cycle's pr_lifecycle phase with dry_run=True (cycle.py:_run_pr_lifecycle_phase <- _run_extended_phases <- run_enterprise_cycle <- autonomy orchestrator <- aria-auto-cycle.yml)'. That chain does not execute. A reader trusting the comment concludes the perimeter is on the scheduled lane, which is precisely how 498 survived review. CLOSED HERE: the superseded invariant deleted (its successor plus test_pr_open_perimeter_callsite cover the behaviour, 10 tests green after deletion; the only remaining reference was .nx/workspace-data/file-map.json, a generated cache artifact, so nothing name-pinned it), and the pr_manager comment corrected in place with the refuted chain quoted so the correction is auditable rather than a silent edit. PLAN CORRECTION recorded rather than followed: RC-8 also specified moving a misplaced `if __name__ == "__main__"` at test_pr_open_perimeter_callsite.py:185 that supposedly made direct execution run only the first test class. That is stale — the guard sits at line 302, after both classes (63 and 212). The plan was written against an earlier state; no move was needed and none was made.

title: The pre-PR-open perimeter authorised dry runs and fed their stage-artifact refusals to the failure breaker, so putting the phase on the live lane would have made the nightly halt itself on its own observations
rule_violated: An observation must not be able to trip a safety breaker. A gate evaluated where the mutation cannot happen is reporting on the stage, not judging the action, and counting its refusals as rejected implementations turns telemetry into a halt condition.
notes: PREVENTATIVE, and the sequencing is the point: this had to land BEFORE RC-1, not after. open_pr_for_action runs the 10-check GATE_PRE_PR_OPEN perimeter before its dry_run branch, deliberately, so a preview cannot skip the gate. But a dry run opens nothing: no changed_files, no base_sha, no diff. Checks needing those refused on data that CANNOT exist at that stage, and cycle.py's _run_pr_lifecycle_phase fed every refusal whose message started with PERIMETER_REFUSED_PREFIX to record_failure(kind='validator_rejection'). Three approved_for_apply proposals in one cycle would trip a breaker that ORPHAN-CRITICAL-420 S2 extended to gate `standard` -- the profile the nightly runs. The lane would halt itself on its own telemetry. It has never fired only because _run_extended_phases is unreachable (ORPHAN-CRITICAL-498), and RC-1 exists to put that phase on the live lane. FIX, tier 1 rather than a flag: the mode is the RESULT TYPE. observe_perimeter() returns a PerimeterObservation with no `passed`, no `failures` and no `raise_if_blocked`, so there is no attribute a breaker producer can read as a refusal; run_hard_fail_checks() keeps its HardFailReport and its fail-closed semantics for real opens. Both run the SAME registry through one implementation, so an observation and an authorisation can never disagree about what a check does. PerimeterVerdict adds a third state, not_evaluable_at_this_stage, distinct from passed=False -- the collapse of those two is what made a dry run look like a rejected implementation. TWO CORRECT ARGUMENTS WERE IN TENSION and neither was discarded: the pre-RC-2 design ran the authorising gate before the dry_run branch so a preview could not report ok while the perimeter would block (a false green), while RC-2 requires that a preview not be counted as a refusal. `evaluable` separates them: a preview is STILL refused when a check that could run refused (self-modification, secret in diff, unsigned commit) and is NOT refused when the only refusals name inputs the stage cannot supply. THE BREAKER IS NOT LEFT WITHOUT A PRODUCER: planner_dispatch_hook records subprocess_timeout from a single except arm, discriminated structurally rather than by message prefix, so ORPHAN-CRITICAL-485 stays closed -- and an invariant pins that, precisely so nobody restores the removed edge believing the breaker went decorative again. ENFORCEMENT: tests/invariants/v3/test_perimeter_observe_has_no_breaker_edge.py, six AST assertions (not grep -- grep is what reported ORPHAN-CRITICAL-428 as wired, and this fix's own comments name record_failure, so a substring version would fail on its documentation). Proven to bite: restoring the edge fails 2 of 6 with the diagnostic naming the phase. Also removed the imports orphaned by the deletion -- an import left behind after its call is what made ORPHAN-HIGH-499's mutation invisible to a hasattr test. The four new public symbols were registered in the v9 __all__ pin rather than the pin being relaxed: that invariant exists to make an API addition a review event.

title: A static reachability invariant cannot catch a kwarg-gated dead pipeline, so the RC-1 tier-3 control does not subsume the tier-1 collapse it was planned alongside
rule_violated: A detection control must be honest about the class of defect it cannot see. Shipping a reachability invariant while the plan describes it as 'the generalised answer to the defect class' would leave readers believing the class is closed when its most expensive instance is invisible to the tool.
notes: FOUND BY BUILDING THE TOOL THE PLAN ASKED FOR. RC-1 specifies a static call-graph reachability invariant and calls it 'the generalised answer to the defect class... the piece that would have caught 494, 495, 497 and the two lens CRITICALs without a review cycle'. It would not have caught ORPHAN-CRITICAL-498, and the reason is structural rather than an implementation gap: a CONDITIONAL call is still an edge. `run_enterprise_cycle` really does call `_run_extended_phases` in the source; the call is guarded by `if run_phases is not None` and no production caller passes the kwarg. Any static walk therefore reports the entire extended pipeline as reachable while it never executes. This is not fixable by improving the resolver -- deciding whether that branch is entered is the halting problem in miniature. CONSEQUENCE FOR SEQUENCING: the tier-3 invariant and the tier-1 collapse cover DIFFERENT failures and neither substitutes for the other. The invariant catches a control with no caller at all (ORPHAN-CRITICAL-420's breaker, whose only occurrence was its own def). The registry catches a control whose caller is never entered (498). Shipping only the invariant and treating RC-1 as closed would leave the more expensive half open under a green test -- the exact shape of the defect class. TWO FALSE POSITIVES ON THE WAY, both from the resolver and both fixed rather than exempted, because a reachability tool that over-reports teaches its readers to ignore it: (1) `record_failure` reported dead, actually reached through callback indirection -- autonomous_planner_dispatcher assigns `invoke_planner = dispatch_one_pending_planner_request` and calls the local, so following imports alone loses the edge; fixed by following single Name = Name aliases. (2) `assert_autonomy_unlocked` reported dead, actually reached through a Protocol-typed strategy OBJECT -- cli -> select_auto_merge_runner -> RealAutoMergeRunner(...) -> runner(...) -> __call__ -> merge_pr_if_ready; fixed by giving a resolved constructor call an edge to that class's __call__, scoped to __call__ alone rather than to every method. Both corrections are documented at the code that makes them. A false accusation is as damaging as a missed defect: acting on either would have meant re-wiring a control that was already wired. CURRENT STATE: all five declared safety controls are reachable from a production entry point, so the invariant's value today is preventing regression, not repairing a present defect. REMAINING WORK, tier 1, design settled and unstarted: a CyclePhase record (name, runner, precondition drawn from an enumerated set), a CYCLE_PHASES ordered tuple as SSoT with pr_lifecycle present under precondition profile_in(PROFILES_WITH_ACTION_AUTHORITY), a uniform PhaseContext so one loop can invoke runners whose signatures currently differ, run_enterprise_cycle iterating that tuple, and run_phases / pre_tool_phases DELETED rather than kept as a compatibility seam -- a second entrance to the same phases is how this happened. Five test files pass those kwargs and migrate with it. Not started in this commit because a half-collapsed pipeline is worse than an uncollapsed one, and the invariant above is what will define 'done' for it: once the kwargs are gone, phase membership is a data question the registry answers.

title: DEFAULT_CYCLE_PHASES declares 5 phases while run_enterprise_cycle runs 15, and one declared name does not match what the body emits, so the phase constants validate a kwarg nobody passes against a list that misdescribes the cycle
rule_violated: A constant that names the steps of a pipeline is either the pipeline's SSoT or it is misinformation. Keeping it as input validation for an argument no production caller passes gives it the appearance of authority with none of the responsibility, and any registry built on it inherits the error.
notes: FOUND WHILE SCOPING RC-1's TIER-1 COLLAPSE, and it changes that work's shape rather than merely adding to it. DECLARED: DEFAULT_CYCLE_PHASES = ('discover','tools','memory','pressure','reflection'), and SUPPORTED_CYCLE_PHASES = that plus architecture_baseline, architecture_postcheck, validation_matrix, pr_lifecycle. ACTUALLY RUN by run_enterprise_cycle's body, enumerated from its own emit_progress calls and post_tool_failure phase labels: belief_decay, consensus_escalation, discovery, human_required_adjudication, judge_calibration, learning_post_evidence_closure, lease_lifecycle_escalation, memory, metrics, observability_dashboard, pressure, proactive_priority, reflection, service_examination, tools -- fifteen, not five. NAME MISMATCH ON TOP: the constant says 'discover' while the body emits 'discovery', so even the one-word overlap is not exact. WHAT THE CONSTANTS ARE FOR: SUPPORTED_CYCLE_PHASES exists only to validate the run_phases / pre_tool_phases kwargs at function entry (cycle.py ~268-281). Those kwargs have no production caller (ORPHAN-CRITICAL-498), so the pair validates input nobody passes, against a phase list that does not describe the cycle. It has the appearance of a phase SSoT and none of the duties of one. CONSEQUENCE FOR RC-1: the plan specifies 'a CYCLE_PHASES ordered tuple as the SSoT' and implicitly treats the existing constant as the set to formalise. Building the registry from those five names would encode the wrong pipeline and leave ten phases outside the SSoT that is supposed to be authoritative -- a duplicate representation, which is the failure the collapse exists to remove. The registry has to be derived from the body's real phases, which makes the collapse materially larger than 'move four extended phases behind preconditions': it is a restructuring of ~300 lines of inline sequential phase code, each block with its own try/except and post_tool_failure assignment. NOT STARTED, deliberately, and this finding is why: a registry built on a constant I have just proven wrong would be worse than no registry. The correct order is (1) settle what the phase set actually is, (2) build CyclePhase / CYCLE_PHASES from that set with enumerated preconditions and an explicit pre_tool/post_tool stage field replacing the two kwargs, (3) delete run_phases, pre_tool_phases, DEFAULT_CYCLE_PHASES and SUPPORTED_CYCLE_PHASES together -- the kwargs and the constants that validate them are one unit and removing either alone leaves a dangling half. A SEPARATE RISK the collapse must handle rather than discover: the four extended phases have NEVER executed in production. Putting them on the live lane runs pr_lifecycle -> open_pr_for_action on every cycle carrying approved_for_apply proposals. ORPHAN-CRITICAL-503 removed the breaker edge so this can no longer self-halt the nightly, but it is still a first-time behaviour change on a scheduled lane and needs its precondition (profile_in(PROFILES_WITH_ACTION_AUTHORITY)) to be right before it is switched on, not after.

title: One undecodable row in the failure ledger trips the breaker permanently: dropped_rows never ages out of the sliding window and the only recovery lever also destroyed the agent queue
rule_violated: A fail-closed safety state must be exitable without discarding evidence. A state that can only be left by deleting the evidence is an outage wearing a safety property's clothes, and it teaches operators to reach for the destructive lever.
notes: MECHANISM, and the ordering that causes it is itself correct. evaluate_breaker decides evidence_incomplete BEFORE the threshold comparison, which is what ORPHAN-CRITICAL-418 fixed: unreadable evidence must not read as permissive. But BreakerEvidence.dropped_rows = max(0, rows_present - len(rows)) counts lines that failed to DECODE, while _count_failures_in_window only ages the lines that DID decode. A corrupt line is therefore outside time: it can never leave the window. One truncated row in aria-tools/breakers/autonomous-failures.jsonl trips the breaker for every subsequent nightly `standard` cycle, permanently. Asserted rather than argued in the new test: re-stamping the surviving row a year into the past leaves the verdict at evidence_incomplete. COMPOUNDING FACTOR: the ledger travels between runs inside the aria-tools-state artifact, and `aria-kernel breaker reset` operates on a local --tools-dir. So the operator's only effective lever was deleting the artifact -- which also destroys the agent-invocation queue ORPHAN-CRITICAL-469 exists to carry. The recovery path for one breaker was the destruction of an unrelated subsystem. FIX, first half, landed: quarantine_breaker_evidence() moves ONLY undecodable rows to a sidecar (verbatim, with an operator-attributed header), keeps every decodable row BYTE-FOR-BYTE, and does NOT touch the state file. The breaker re-derives from the survivors. So the state becomes EVALUABLE, not clear -- and the test that matters asserts exactly that: three real in-window failures plus one corrupt line quarantines to a breaker that is STILL tripped, now with reason threshold_exceeded, which is what the operator needed to see all along. A reset would have cleared both, which is why this is a different verb rather than a flag on reset: an operator reaching for 'make the breaker evaluable' must not land on 'discard the evidence'. It refuses on a count mismatch between its own per-line partition and the breaker's own read_strict_jsonl reader, because rewriting the ledger against a different definition of decodable than the evaluator uses would be two sites disagreeing about one file. It refuses outright when the ledger is unreadable -- that is a file-access fault, not row damage, and rewriting a file we could not read would be writing over evidence never seen. It gets a CLI (`aria-kernel breaker quarantine --acknowledge --reason ... --operator-approval-ref ...`) because ORPHAN-HIGH-465 was precisely an operator-recovery function shipped with no command surface; exit 1 when the breaker is still tripped afterwards, so a still-blocked lane cannot read as a finished recovery. NOT DONE, second half: recovery still runs where the state ISN'T. The CLI operates on a local --tools-dir while the live ledger lives in the artifact, so an operator cannot yet quarantine the deployed ledger. The design is a workflow_dispatch input on aria-agent-executor performing restore -> mutate -> republish THROUGH THE EXISTING S1 BRIDGE (ORPHAN-CRITICAL-469) -- explicitly not a second restore path, because a duplicate transaction around a hash-chained ledger is how the ledger diverges. Not implemented here because it needs a live artifact round-trip to verify and this container cannot reach the GitHub API; shipping it unverified would be the untested-callsite defect this whole branch exists to close.

title: The spec type-check ratchet enumerated three hardcoded roots and so never covered tests/invariants: 24 pre-existing type errors in the files that enforce every other platform rule were invisible to every gate
rule_violated: A gate's coverage set must be derived from the property that makes something coverable, not from a hand-maintained list of places to look. An enumerated root list is a log of the times someone noticed, so the first directory nobody noticed is silently ungated — and the gate still reports OK.
notes: FOUND BY CHASING A SYMPTOM I HAD MIS-DIAGNOSED. Earlier in this session I flagged that 'two type gates disagree about one tree' after CI - Full's type-check step passed on commit 4aa3309e1 while Quality Gates' type-check job failed with three noUncheckedIndexedAccess errors in tests/invariants/git-hook-binding.spec.ts. On investigation the scopes are DELIBERATE and layered, not contradictory: tools/scripts/type-check-all.mjs covers app/lib COMPILE tsconfigs and documents that it excludes .spec.json ('tests are a separate concern'); gates:type-check-spec owns spec tsconfigs as a baseline-aware ratchet; ci-affected's scripts/ci/type-check-changed-files.mjs covers CHANGED files anywhere. So my original framing was wrong and is withdrawn. THE REAL DEFECT, one layer down: type-check-spec.ts discoverProjects() enumerated roots = ['apps','libs','platform/libs'], and its own comment recorded that platform/libs had been appended the first time a platform lib grew a spec config -- which is the tell. The list is a log of the times someone noticed. MEASURED: the repo holds 30 tsconfig.spec.json files; those three roots reach 29. The one missed is tests/invariants -- the directory holding the invariants that enforce every other rule in the platform, so the ratchet that guards spec type errors was blind to the specs that guard everything else. CONSEQUENCE: a type error there was caught only by ci-affected's changed-files guard, which sees a file when it CHANGES and never guards the rest, so a PRE-EXISTING error was invisible to every gate. That is exactly why my own error surfaced in one lane and not the other. FIX: discoverProjects() now DERIVES the project set from the presence of a tsconfig.spec.json via a depth-bounded walk, stopping descent at a project so a nested fixture config cannot register as its own entry. A new top-level tree is covered the moment it acquires a spec config, with no second place to remember to edit. Proven to bite on the newly covered project: injecting one error reports 'tests/invariants 25 (baseline 24, +1) regressed' and fails the gate. WHAT WAS NOT DONE, and why. Widening the gate revealed 24 pre-existing errors across SIX invariant files I did not write (aria-workflow-sha-pin, rls-predicate-canonical, pii-events-mandatory-crypto-shred, migration-registration-completeness, event-contract-emit-has-interface, dead-contract-fe-operations), all of the same class: undefined-not-assignable under noUncheckedIndexedAccess. They are recorded as the project's baseline (24), which is the ratchet's designed onboarding path and identical to how 11 of 20 projects were onboarded when the gate was introduced. That makes 24 invisible errors into 24 tracked-and-capped errors -- a strict improvement and tier 3, NOT tier 1. The errors themselves are not fixed: doing it correctly means reading six unfamiliar invariant files, and the shortcuts available (non-null assertions, casts) are banned by CLAUDE.md and would be worse than the debt. Owner and deadline recorded here for that cleanup; the ratchet guarantees the number cannot grow while it waits.

title: No local git hook type-checked anything: pre-commit ran staged-only gates and pre-push ran only Rust clippy, so a TypeScript error could only be discovered by CI
rule_violated: A gate that blocks merge in CI needs a local counterpart that fires earlier, and the parity mechanism that enforces this must cover every kind of gate — not one family. A parity invariant that understands only one gate type teaches its readers that parity is enforced everywhere.
notes: MEASURED CONSEQUENCE, from this session. A noUncheckedIndexedAccess error in tests/invariants/git-hook-binding.spec.ts reached CI on PR #1024 head 4aa3309e1 and failed the type-check job, taking merge-gate and sens-enterprise-summary down with it as derivatives. I had verified the file with jest, which transpiles without full type-checking, so the suite was green while tsc --noEmit was not. No local hook could have caught it: .husky/pre-commit runs staged-only banned-phrase/construct/migration/tier-claim gates plus the format gate, and .husky/pre-push ran ONE thing -- tools/gates/clippy-affected.ts. TypeScript had no local gate at all. Same missing-local-mirror shape as ORPHAN-HIGH-500, one gate over. FIX, and the choice of WHICH gate to mirror is the architectural part. Platform-wide `npm run type-check` takes ~2.5 minutes; adding that to every push makes people look for ways around the hook, and a hook people bypass is worse than no hook. So the mirror is the gate that actually catches this class in CI: ci-affected's scripts/ci/type-check-changed-files.mjs. Its cost is proportional to the change and its scope is exactly the risky set. Wired into pre-push, which is the correct stage because the script compares a COMMITTED range (origin/main..HEAD) -- pre-commit content is not committed yet, so the same script there would compare the wrong pair. When origin/main cannot be resolved it skips LOUDLY, printing why: a base that cannot be computed means 'changed' is undefined, and blocking an offline branch push would be wrong -- but skipping silently is the blind-gate defect this session already fixed once, so the reason is printed and CI remains the authority. SECOND HALF OF THE FIX, and the reason this finding is not just 'add a hook line': the parity invariant added for ORPHAN-HIGH-500 understood only `quality.mjs <domain> <action>` gates. It enforced parity for exactly one family and silently ignored every other kind of CI gate -- the same shape as ORPHAN-HIGH-507's hardcoded root list, one layer up. It now also asserts a declared set of SCRIPT gates, matched on script PATH rather than command line so a hook passing different arguments than CI (pre-push uses --base origin/main; CI uses the PR base ref) still counts as the mirror. The set is declared rather than 'every script any workflow runs', because most CI steps -- builds, uploads, container setup -- have no business in a git hook and asserting they do would make the invariant noise; what belongs is a gate that REFUSES a change on a property a developer could have checked locally. Proven to bite: deleting the pre-push line fails the new assertion naming the script and the reason it exists.

title: The workflow-injection invariant matched only the legacy ${{ github.event.inputs.X }} spelling, so a run: block interpolating the modern ${{ inputs.X }} shorthand passed a green gate
rule_violated: A gate that recognises one spelling of the construct it forbids enforces half its rule while reporting full compliance. Where a language offers two syntaxes for the same value, the gate must match the VALUE, not the syntax someone happened to write when the gate was authored.
notes: FOUND BY DISTRUSTING MY OWN GREEN RESULT. While adding the RC-9 capability probe I wrote `echo "${{ inputs.runner_label }}"` inside a run: block -- textbook shell injection of operator-supplied text. The repo HAS an invariant for exactly this (Plan 024 v3 B-3, aria-workflow-input-injection.spec.ts) and it PASSED on my file. Rather than accept the pass I checked why, expecting the same hardcoded-list defect as ORPHAN-HIGH-507. It was not that -- the spec scans every workflow via readdirSync, which is correct. The defect was the pattern: INPUTS_INTERPOLATION_RE matched only /\$\{\{\s*github\.event\.inputs\.[A-Za-z0-9_]+\s*\}\}/, the LEGACY spelling. GitHub also offers `${{ inputs.X }}` as the modern workflow_dispatch shorthand; both splice the same attacker-controlled value into the same shell, and the gate recognised one of them. So the invariant reported compliance on a file that violated the rule it exists to enforce. FIXED IN THE SAME CHANGE as the workflow that exposed it: the pattern now matches both spellings, the offending workflow passes its input through an `env:` block and references "$VAR" (the canonical fix the spec's own docstring prescribes), and the test TITLE was corrected too -- it named only `${{ github.event.inputs.* }}`, which is the same misinformation one layer up: a reader scanning test names would conclude the modern spelling was out of scope by design. Proven to bite both ways: with the fix in place the suite is green, and restoring `${{ inputs.runner_label }}` inside the run: block fails the invariant with the file, line and matched snippet. RESIDUAL, stated because it bounds the fix: the invariant's scope is deliberately limited to aria-* workflows (its docstring says non-ARIA workflows are tracked separately as ORPHAN-HIGH findings for the platform-CI plan). This change widens WHICH SPELLINGS are caught, not WHICH FILES are scanned, so a non-ARIA workflow interpolating either spelling is still outside this gate -- unchanged by this fix and not silently implied to be covered.

title: The ARIA kernel suite is the gate that catches ARIA regressions and it had no local counterpart of any kind, so both git hooks reported green on a commit with four red tests and that commit was pushed
rule_violated: CLAUDE.md's 'never commit with red tests' is a rule about outcomes, and an outcome rule with no mechanism behind it is enforced by whoever happens to remember. A CI gate whose failures are only visible after a push is a gate the author learns about from the wrong side of history they cannot rewrite.
